# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0.15/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

# enum_iterator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enum-iterator/latest/target-redirect/enum_iterator/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Tools to iterate over the values of a type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, first, last, next, previous, reverse_all, Sequence};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
assert_eq!(cardinality::<Day>(), 7);
assert_eq!(all::<Day>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
    Day::Monday,
    Day::Tuesday,
    Day::Wednesday,
    Day::Thursday,
    Day::Friday,
    Day::Saturday,
    Day::Sunday,
]);
assert_eq!(first::<Day>(), Some(Day::Monday));
assert_eq!(last::<Day>(), Some(Day::Sunday));
assert_eq!(next(&Day::Tuesday), Some(Day::Wednesday));
assert_eq!(previous(&Day::Wednesday), Some(Day::Tuesday));
assert_eq!(reverse_all::<Day>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
    Day::Sunday,
    Day::Saturday,
    Day::Friday,
    Day::Thursday,
    Day::Wednesday,
    Day::Tuesday,
    Day::Monday,
]);
```
```
use enum_iterator::{cardinality, first, last, Sequence};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
struct Foo {
    a: bool,
    b: u8,
}
assert_eq!(cardinality::<Foo>(), 512);
assert_eq!(first::<Foo>(), Some(Foo { a: false, b: 0 }));
assert_eq!(last::<Foo>(), Some(Foo { a: true, b: 255 }));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-crate-path-in-generated-code)Custom crate path in generated code

The code generated by the derive macro defaults to using `::enum_iterator` as the path for
items defined in this crate. This can be customized using the
`#[enum_iterator(crate = foo::bar)]` derive macro attribute.

```
#[derive(enum_iterator::Sequence)]
#[enum_iterator(crate = enum_iterator)]
struct Foo;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust version

This crate tracks stable Rust. Minor releases may require a newer Rust version. Patch releases must not require a newer Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribute)Contribute

All contributions shall be licensed under the [0BSD license](https://spdx.org/licenses/0BSD.html).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [All](https://docs.rs/struct.All.html)
- Iterator over the values of type `T`.
- [Reverse](https://docs.rs/struct.ReverseAll.html)- All
- Iterator over the values of type `T`in reverse order.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Sequence](https://docs.rs/trait.Sequence.html)
- Trait to iterate over the values of a type.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [all](https://docs.rs/fn.all.html)
- Returns an iterator over all values of type `T`.
- [cardinality](https://docs.rs/fn.cardinality.html)
- Returns the cardinality (number of values) of `T`
- [first](https://docs.rs/fn.first.html)
- Returns the first value of type `T`.
- [last](https://docs.rs/fn.last.html)
- Returns the last value of type `T`.
- [next](https://docs.rs/fn.next.html)
- Returns the next value of type `T`or`None`if this was the end.
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_cycle.html)- cycle
- Returns the next value of type `T`or`first()`
- [previous](https://docs.rs/fn.previous.html)
- Returns the previous value of type `T`or`None`if this was the beginning.
- [previous_](https://docs.rs/fn.previous_cycle.html)- cycle
- Returns the previous value of type `T`or`last()`
- [reverse_](https://docs.rs/fn.reverse_all.html)- all
- Returns an iterator over all values of type `T`in the reverse order of`all`

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Sequence](https://docs.rs/derive.Sequence.html)
- Derives `Sequence`.

[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// use enum_iterator::{previous_cycle, Sequence};
[193](https://docs.rs#193)///
[194](https://docs.rs#194)/// #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)/// enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)///
[197](https://docs.rs#197)/// assert_eq!(previous_cycle(&Day::Monday), Day::Sunday);
[198](https://docs.rs#198)/// ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)pub fn previous_cycle<T: Sequence>(x: &T) -> T {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    previous(x)
[201](https://docs.rs#201)        .or_else(last)
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        .expect("Sequence::last returned None for inhabited type")
[203](https://docs.rs#203)}

[274](https://docs.rs#274)
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// Trait to iterate over the values of a type.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// The [crate root](crate) defines useful functions to work with types implementing `Sequence`.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)///
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// # Derivation
[280](https://docs.rs#280)///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)/// `Sequence` can be derived for `enum` and `struct` types. Specifically, it can be derived
[282](https://docs.rs#282)/// for:
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// - Enumerations whose variants meet one of the following criteria:
[284](https://docs.rs#284)///   - The variant does not have fields.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)///   - The variant has fields meeting all these conditions:
[286](https://docs.rs#286)///     - Every field has a type that implements `Sequence`.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)///     - Every field but the last one has a type that implements `Clone`.
[288](https://docs.rs#288)/// - Enumerations without variants.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)/// - Structures whose fields meet all these conditions:
[290](https://docs.rs#290)///     - Every field has a type that implements `Sequence`.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///     - Every field but the last one has a type that implements `Clone`.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// - Unit structures (i.e. without fields).
[293](https://docs.rs#293)///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// The cardinality (number of values) of the type must not exceed `usize::MAX`.
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// # Laws
[297](https://docs.rs#297)///
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// `T: Sequence` implies the following assertions:
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// - `T::first().and_then(|x| x.previous()).is_none()`
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// - `T::last().and_then(|x| x.next()).is_none()`
[301](https://docs.rs#301)/// - `T::first().is_none()` ⇔ `T::last().is_none()`
[302](https://docs.rs#302)/// - `std::iter::successors(T::first(), T::next)` must eventually yield `T::last()`.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)/// - If `T` is inhabited, `T::first().is_some()`.
[304](https://docs.rs#304)///
[305](https://docs.rs#305)/// If a manual implementation of `Sequence` violates any of these laws, the functions at the crate root may misbehave, including panicking.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)/// # Examples
[308](https://docs.rs#308)/// ## C-like enumeration
[309](https://docs.rs#309)///
[310](https://docs.rs#310)/// ```
[311](https://docs.rs#311)/// use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, Sequence};
[312](https://docs.rs#312)///
[313](https://docs.rs#313)/// #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[314](https://docs.rs#314)/// enum Direction { North, South, West, East }
[315](https://docs.rs#315)///
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// assert_eq!(cardinality::<Direction>(), 4);
[317](https://docs.rs#317)/// assert_eq!(all::<Direction>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
[318](https://docs.rs#318)///     Direction::North,
[319](https://docs.rs#319)///     Direction::South,
[320](https://docs.rs#320)///     Direction::West,
[321](https://docs.rs#321)///     Direction::East,
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// ]);
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// ```
[324](https://docs.rs#324)///
[325](https://docs.rs#325)/// ## Enumeration with data
[326](https://docs.rs#326)///
[327](https://docs.rs#327)/// ```
[328](https://docs.rs#328)/// use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, Sequence};
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// enum Direction { North, South, West, East }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)///
[333](https://docs.rs#333)/// #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[334](https://docs.rs#334)/// enum Greeting {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)///     Hi,
[336](https://docs.rs#336)///     Bye,
[337](https://docs.rs#337)/// }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)///
[339](https://docs.rs#339)/// #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[340](https://docs.rs#340)/// enum Action {
[341](https://docs.rs#341)///     Move(Direction),
[342](https://docs.rs#342)///     Jump,
[343](https://docs.rs#343)///     Talk { greeting: Greeting, loud: bool },
[344](https://docs.rs#344)/// }
[345](https://docs.rs#345)///
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// assert_eq!(cardinality::<Action>(), 4 + 1 + 2 * 2);
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// assert_eq!(all::<Action>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
[348](https://docs.rs#348)///     Action::Move(Direction::North),
[349](https://docs.rs#349)///     Action::Move(Direction::South),
[350](https://docs.rs#350)///     Action::Move(Direction::West),
[351](https://docs.rs#351)///     Action::Move(Direction::East),
[352](https://docs.rs#352)///     Action::Jump,
[353](https://docs.rs#353)///     Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Hi, loud: false },
[354](https://docs.rs#354)///     Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Hi, loud: true },
[355](https://docs.rs#355)///     Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Bye, loud: false },
[356](https://docs.rs#356)///     Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Bye, loud: true },
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// ]);
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// ```
[359](https://docs.rs#359)///
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// ## Structure
[361](https://docs.rs#361)///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)/// ```
[363](https://docs.rs#363)/// use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, Sequence};
[364](https://docs.rs#364)///
[365](https://docs.rs#365)/// #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[366](https://docs.rs#366)/// enum Side {
[367](https://docs.rs#367)///     Left,
[368](https://docs.rs#368)///     Right,
[369](https://docs.rs#369)/// }
[370](https://docs.rs#370)///
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[372](https://docs.rs#372)/// enum LimbKind {
[373](https://docs.rs#373)///     Arm,
[374](https://docs.rs#374)///     Leg,
[375](https://docs.rs#375)/// }
[376](https://docs.rs#376)///
[377](https://docs.rs#377)/// #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// struct Limb {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)///     kind: LimbKind,
[380](https://docs.rs#380)///     side: Side,
[381](https://docs.rs#381)/// }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)///
[383](https://docs.rs#383)/// assert_eq!(cardinality::<Limb>(), 4);
[384](https://docs.rs#384)/// assert_eq!(all::<Limb>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
[385](https://docs.rs#385)///     Limb { kind: LimbKind::Arm, side: Side::Left },
[386](https://docs.rs#386)///     Limb { kind: LimbKind::Arm, side: Side::Right },
[387](https://docs.rs#387)///     Limb { kind: LimbKind::Leg, side: Side::Left },
[388](https://docs.rs#388)///     Limb { kind: LimbKind::Leg, side: Side::Right },
[389](https://docs.rs#389)/// ]);
[390](https://docs.rs#390)/// ```
[391](https://docs.rs#391)pub trait Sequence: Sized {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// Number of values of type `Self`.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// # Example
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// ```
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// use enum_iterator::Sequence;
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// #[derive(Sequence)]
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    ///
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// assert_eq!(Day::CARDINALITY, 7);
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// ```
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    const CARDINALITY: usize;
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// Returns value following `*self` or `None` if this was the end.
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    ///
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// Values are yielded in the following order. Comparisons between values are based on their
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// relative order as yielded by `next`; an element yielded after another is considered greater.
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    ///
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// - For primitive types, in increasing order (same as `Ord`).
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// - For arrays and tuples, in lexicographic order of the sequence of their elements.
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// - When derived for an enumeration, in variant definition order.
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// - When derived for a structure, in lexicographic order of the sequence of its fields taken
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///   in definition order.
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    ///
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// The order described above is the same as `Ord` if any custom `Sequence` implementation
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// follows `Ord` and any enumeration has its variants defined in increasing order of
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// discriminant.
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// # Example
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// ```
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    /// use enum_iterator::Sequence;
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    ///
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    ///
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    /// assert_eq!(Day::Tuesday.next(), Some(Day::Wednesday));
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// ```
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    fn next(&self) -> Option<Self>;
[430](https://docs.rs#430)
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// Returns value preceding `*self` or `None` if this was the beginning.
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    ///
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    /// # Example
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// ```
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// use enum_iterator::Sequence;
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    ///
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    ///
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// assert_eq!(Day::Wednesday.previous(), Some(Day::Tuesday));
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// ```
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    fn previous(&self) -> Option<Self>;
[443](https://docs.rs#443)
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// Returns the first value of type `Self`.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    ///
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// # Example
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    /// ```
[448](https://docs.rs#448)    /// use enum_iterator::Sequence;
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    ///
[450](https://docs.rs#450)    /// #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    ///
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    /// assert_eq!(Day::first(), Some(Day::Monday));
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// ```
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    fn first() -> Option<Self>;
[456](https://docs.rs#456)
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    /// Returns the last value of type `Self`.
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    ///
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    /// # Example
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// ```
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    /// use enum_iterator::Sequence;
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    ///
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    /// #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    ///
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    /// assert_eq!(Day::last(), Some(Day::Sunday));
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// ```
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    fn last() -> Option<Self>;
[469](https://docs.rs#469)}
[470](https://docs.rs#470)
[471](https://docs.rs#471)impl Sequence for bool {
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    const CARDINALITY: usize = 2;
[473](https://docs.rs#473)
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    fn next(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        (!*self).then_some(true)
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)

[483](https://docs.rs#483)        Some(false)
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    }
[485](https://docs.rs#485)
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    fn last() -> Option<Self> {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)        Some(true)
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    }

[510](https://docs.rs#510)            }

[560](https://docs.rs#560)impl Sequence for Ordering {
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    const CARDINALITY: usize = 3;
[562](https://docs.rs#562)
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    fn next(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[564](https://docs.rs#564)        int_to_ordering(*self as i8 + 1)
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    }
[566](https://docs.rs#566)
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    fn previous(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[568](https://docs.rs#568)        int_to_ordering(*self as i8 - 1)
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    }
[570](https://docs.rs#570)
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    fn first() -> Option<Self> {
[572](https://docs.rs#572)        Some(Ordering::Less)
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    fn last() -> Option<Self> {
[576](https://docs.rs#576)        Some(Ordering::Greater)
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    }

[579](https://docs.rs#579)
[580](https://docs.rs#580)fn int_to_ordering(i: i8) -> Option<Ordering> {
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    match i {
[582](https://docs.rs#582)        -1 => Some(Ordering::Less),
[583](https://docs.rs#583)        0 => Some(Ordering::Equal),
[584](https://docs.rs#584)        1 => Some(Ordering::Greater),
[585](https://docs.rs#585)        _ => None,
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    }
[587](https://docs.rs#587)}

[589](https://docs.rs#589)impl<T: Sequence> Sequence for Option<T> {
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    const CARDINALITY: usize = T::CARDINALITY + 1;

[592](https://docs.rs#592)    fn next(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[593](https://docs.rs#593)        match self {
[594](https://docs.rs#594)            None => T::first().map(Some),
[595](https://docs.rs#595)            Some(x) => x.next().map(Some),
[596](https://docs.rs#596)        }

[598](https://docs.rs#598)
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    fn previous(&self) -> Option<Self> {

[612](https://docs.rs#612)impl<T: Sequence> Sequence for Poll<T> {

[614](https://docs.rs#614)
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    fn next(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[616](https://docs.rs#616)        match self {
[617](https://docs.rs#617)            Poll::Ready(x) => x.next().map(Poll::Ready).or(Some(Poll::Pending)),
[618](https://docs.rs#618)            Poll::Pending => None,
[619](https://docs.rs#619)        }
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    }
[621](https://docs.rs#621)
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    fn previous(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[623](https://docs.rs#623)        match self {
[624](https://docs.rs#624)            Poll::Ready(x) => x.previous().map(Poll::Ready),
[625](https://docs.rs#625)            Poll::Pending => T::last().map(Poll::Ready),
[626](https://docs.rs#626)        }
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    }
[628](https://docs.rs#628)
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    fn first() -> Option<Self> {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)        T::first().map(Poll::Ready).or(Some(Poll::Pending))
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    }
[632](https://docs.rs#632)
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    fn last() -> Option<Self> {
[634](https://docs.rs#634)        Some(Poll::Pending)
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    }

[638](https://docs.rs#638)impl<const N: usize, T: Sequence + Clone> Sequence for [T; N] {
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    const CARDINALITY: usize = {
[640](https://docs.rs#640)        let tc = T::CARDINALITY;
[641](https://docs.rs#641)        let mut c = 1;
[642](https://docs.rs#642)        let mut i = 0;
[643](https://docs.rs#643)        loop {
[644](https://docs.rs#644)            if i == N {
[645](https://docs.rs#645)                break c;
[646](https://docs.rs#646)            }
[647](https://docs.rs#647)            c *= tc;
[648](https://docs.rs#648)            i += 1;
[649](https://docs.rs#649)        }
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    };
[651](https://docs.rs#651)
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    fn next(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[653](https://docs.rs#653)        advance_for_array(self, T::first)
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    }
[655](https://docs.rs#655)
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    fn previous(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[657](https://docs.rs#657)        advance_for_array(self, T::last)
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    }
[659](https://docs.rs#659)
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    fn first() -> Option<Self> {
[661](https://docs.rs#661)        if N == 0 {
[662](https://docs.rs#662)            Some(core::array::from_fn(|_| unreachable!()))
[663](https://docs.rs#663)        } else {
[664](https://docs.rs#664)            let x = T::first()?;
[665](https://docs.rs#665)            Some(core::array::from_fn(|_| x.clone()))
[666](https://docs.rs#666)        }
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    }
[668](https://docs.rs#668)
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    fn last() -> Option<Self> {
[670](https://docs.rs#670)        if N == 0 {
[671](https://docs.rs#671)            Some(core::array::from_fn(|_| unreachable!()))
[672](https://docs.rs#672)        } else {
[673](https://docs.rs#673)            let x = T::last()?;
[674](https://docs.rs#674)            Some(core::array::from_fn(|_| x.clone()))
[675](https://docs.rs#675)        }
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    }
[677](https://docs.rs#677)}
[678](https://docs.rs#678)
[679](https://docs.rs#679)fn advance_for_array<const N: usize, T, R>(a: &[T; N], reset: R) -> Option<[T; N]>
[680](https://docs.rs#680)where
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    T: Sequence + Clone,
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    R: Fn() -> Option<T>,
[683](https://docs.rs#683){
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    let mut a = a.clone();
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    let keep = a.iter_mut().rev().try_fold((), |_, x| match x.next() {
[686](https://docs.rs#686)        Some(new_x) => {
[687](https://docs.rs#687)            *x = new_x;
[688](https://docs.rs#688)            ControlFlow::Break(true)
[689](https://docs.rs#689)        }
[690](https://docs.rs#690)        None => match reset() {
[691](https://docs.rs#691)            Some(new_x) => {
[692](https://docs.rs#692)                *x = new_x;
[693](https://docs.rs#693)                ControlFlow::Continue(())
[694](https://docs.rs#694)            }
[695](https://docs.rs#695)            None => ControlFlow::Break(false),
[696](https://docs.rs#696)        },
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    });
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    Some(a).filter(|_| matches!(keep, ControlFlow::Break(true)))
[699](https://docs.rs#699)}

[701](https://docs.rs#701)macro_rules! impl_seq_advance_for_tuple {
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    (
[703](https://docs.rs#703)        $this:ident,
[704](https://docs.rs#704)        $advance:ident,
[705](https://docs.rs#705)        $reset:ident,
[706](https://docs.rs#706)        $carry:ident
[707](https://docs.rs#707)        @ $($values:expr,)*
[708](https://docs.rs#708)        @
[709](https://docs.rs#709)        @ $($placeholders:pat,)*
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    ) => {
[711](https://docs.rs#711)        Some(($($values,)*)).filter(|_| !$carry)
[712](https://docs.rs#712)    };
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    (
[714](https://docs.rs#714)        $this:ident,
[715](https://docs.rs#715)        $advance:ident,
[716](https://docs.rs#716)        $reset:ident,
[717](https://docs.rs#717)        $carry:ident
[718](https://docs.rs#718)        @ $($values:expr,)*
[719](https://docs.rs#719)        @ $ty:ident, $($types:ident,)*
[720](https://docs.rs#720)        @ $($placeholders:pat,)*
[721](https://docs.rs#721)    ) => {{
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        let (.., item, $($placeholders,)*) = $this;
[723](https://docs.rs#723)        let (x, new_carry) = if $carry {
[724](https://docs.rs#724)            match Sequence::$advance(item) {
[725](https://docs.rs#725)                Some(x) => (x, false),
[726](https://docs.rs#726)                None => (Sequence::$reset()?, true),
[727](https://docs.rs#727)            }
[728](https://docs.rs#728)        } else {
[729](https://docs.rs#729)            (item.clone(), false)
[730](https://docs.rs#730)        };
[731](https://docs.rs#731)        impl_seq_advance_for_tuple!(
[732](https://docs.rs#732)            $this,
[733](https://docs.rs#733)            $advance,
[734](https://docs.rs#734)            $reset,
[735](https://docs.rs#735)            new_carry
[736](https://docs.rs#736)            @ x, $($values,)*
[737](https://docs.rs#737)            @ $($types,)*
[738](https://docs.rs#738)            @ _, $($placeholders,)*
[739](https://docs.rs#739)        )
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    }};
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    ($this:ident, $advance:ident, $reset:ident @ $($types:ident,)*) => {{
[742](https://docs.rs#742)        let (.., item) = $this;
[743](https://docs.rs#743)        let (x, carry) = match Sequence::$advance(item) {
[744](https://docs.rs#744)            Some(x) => (x, false),
[745](https://docs.rs#745)            None => (Sequence::$reset()?, true),
[746](https://docs.rs#746)        };
[747](https://docs.rs#747)        impl_seq_advance_for_tuple!($this, $advance, $reset, carry @ x, @ $($types,)* @ _,)
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    }};
[749](https://docs.rs#749)}

[751](https://docs.rs#751)macro_rules! impl_sequence_for_tuple {
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    ($($types:ident,)* @ $last:ident) => {
[753](https://docs.rs#753)        impl<$($types,)* $last> Sequence for ($($types,)* $last,)
[754](https://docs.rs#754)        where
[755](https://docs.rs#755)            $($types: Sequence + Clone,)*
[756](https://docs.rs#756)            $last: Sequence,
[757](https://docs.rs#757)        {
[758](https://docs.rs#758)            const CARDINALITY: usize =
[759](https://docs.rs#759)                $(<$types as Sequence>::CARDINALITY *)* <$last as Sequence>::CARDINALITY;
[760](https://docs.rs#760)
[761](https://docs.rs#761)            fn next(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[762](https://docs.rs#762)                impl_seq_advance_for_tuple!(self, next, first @ $($types,)*)
[763](https://docs.rs#763)            }
[764](https://docs.rs#764)
[765](https://docs.rs#765)            fn previous(&self) -> Option<Self> {
[766](https://docs.rs#766)                impl_seq_advance_for_tuple!(self, previous, last @ $($types,)*)
[767](https://docs.rs#767)            }
[768](https://docs.rs#768)
[769](https://docs.rs#769)            fn first() -> Option<Self> {
[770](https://docs.rs#770)                Some((
[771](https://docs.rs#771)                    $(<$types as Sequence>::first()?,)*
[772](https://docs.rs#772)                    <$last as Sequence>::first()?,
[773](https://docs.rs#773)                ))
[774](https://docs.rs#774)            }
[775](https://docs.rs#775)
[776](https://docs.rs#776)            fn last() -> Option<Self> {
[777](https://docs.rs#777)                Some((
[778](https://docs.rs#778)                    $(<$types as Sequence>::last()?,)*
[779](https://docs.rs#779)                    <$last as Sequence>::last()?,
[780](https://docs.rs#780)                ))
[781](https://docs.rs#781)            }
[782](https://docs.rs#782)        }
[783](https://docs.rs#783)    };
[784](https://docs.rs#784)}
[785](https://docs.rs#785)

# Sequence in enum_iterator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enum-iterator/latest/target-redirect/enum_iterator/trait.Sequence.html

`pub trait Sequence: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    const [CARDINALITY](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.CARDINALITY): [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html);
    // Required methods
    fn [next](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>;
[previous](https://docs.rs#tymethod.previous)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>;
[first](https://docs.rs#tymethod.first)() -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>;
[last](https://docs.rs#tymethod.last)() -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>;
}## Expand description

Trait to iterate over the values of a type.

The [crate root](https://docs.rs/index.html) defines useful functions to work with types implementing `Sequence`.

[§](https://docs.rs#derivation)Derivation

`Sequence` can be derived for `enum` and `struct` types. Specifically, it can be derived
for:

- Enumerations whose variants meet one of the following criteria:
- The variant does not have fields.
- The variant has fields meeting all these conditions:
- Every field has a type that implements `Sequence`.
- Every field but the last one has a type that implements `Clone`.

- Every field has a type that implements

- Enumerations without variants.
- Structures whose fields meet all these conditions:
- Every field has a type that implements `Sequence`.
- Every field but the last one has a type that implements `Clone`.

- Every field has a type that implements
- Unit structures (i.e. without fields).

The cardinality (number of values) of the type must not exceed `usize::MAX`.

[§](https://docs.rs#laws)Laws

`T: Sequence` implies the following assertions:

- `T::first().and_then(|x| x.previous()).is_none()`
- `T::last().and_then(|x| x.next()).is_none()`
- `T::first().is_none()`⇔- `T::last().is_none()`
- `std::iter::successors(T::first(), T::next)`must eventually yield- `T::last()`.
- If `T`is inhabited,`T::first().is_some()`.

If a manual implementation of `Sequence` violates any of these laws, the functions at the crate root may misbehave, including panicking.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#c-like-enumeration)C-like enumeration

```
use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, Sequence};
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Direction { North, South, West, East }
assert_eq!(cardinality::<Direction>(), 4);
assert_eq!(all::<Direction>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
    Direction::North,
    Direction::South,
    Direction::West,
    Direction::East,
]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#enumeration-with-data)Enumeration with data

```
use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, Sequence};
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Direction { North, South, West, East }
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Greeting {
    Hi,
    Bye,
}
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Action {
    Move(Direction),
    Jump,
    Talk { greeting: Greeting, loud: bool },
}
assert_eq!(cardinality::<Action>(), 4 + 1 + 2 * 2);
assert_eq!(all::<Action>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
    Action::Move(Direction::North),
    Action::Move(Direction::South),
    Action::Move(Direction::West),
    Action::Move(Direction::East),
    Action::Jump,
    Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Hi, loud: false },
    Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Hi, loud: true },
    Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Bye, loud: false },
    Action::Talk { greeting: Greeting::Bye, loud: true },
]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#structure)Structure

```
use enum_iterator::{all, cardinality, Sequence};
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Side {
    Left,
    Right,
}
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum LimbKind {
    Arm,
    Leg,
}
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
struct Limb {
    kind: LimbKind,
    side: Side,
}
assert_eq!(cardinality::<Limb>(), 4);
assert_eq!(all::<Limb>().collect::<Vec<_>>(), [
    Limb { kind: LimbKind::Arm, side: Side::Left },
    Limb { kind: LimbKind::Arm, side: Side::Right },
    Limb { kind: LimbKind::Leg, side: Side::Left },
    Limb { kind: LimbKind::Leg, side: Side::Right },
]);
```
## Required Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-consts)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Returns value following `*self` or `None` if this was the end.

Values are yielded in the following order. Comparisons between values are based on their
relative order as yielded by `next`; an element yielded after another is considered greater.

- For primitive types, in increasing order (same as `Ord`).
- For arrays and tuples, in lexicographic order of the sequence of their elements.
- When derived for an enumeration, in variant definition order.
- When derived for a structure, in lexicographic order of the sequence of its fields taken in definition order.

The order described above is the same as `Ord` if any custom `Sequence` implementation
follows `Ord` and any enumeration has its variants defined in increasing order of
discriminant.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use enum_iterator::Sequence;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
assert_eq!(Day::Tuesday.next(), Some(Day::Wednesday));
```
Returns value preceding `*self` or `None` if this was the beginning.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
use enum_iterator::Sequence;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
assert_eq!(Day::Wednesday.previous(), Some(Day::Tuesday));
```

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# all in enum_iterator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enum-iterator/latest/target-redirect/enum_iterator/fn.all.html

## Expand description

Returns an iterator over all values of type `T`.

Values are yielded in the order defined by [ Sequence::next](https://docs.rs/trait.Sequence.html#tymethod.next), starting with

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Sequence.html#tymethod.first)

`Sequence::first`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enum_iterator::{all, Sequence};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }
assert_eq!(
    all::<Color>().collect::<Vec<_>>(),
    [Color::Red, Color::Green, Color::Blue],
);
```

---

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enum-iterator/latest/target-redirect/enum_iterator/fn.cardinality.html

use enum_iterator::{cardinality, Sequence};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }
assert_eq!(cardinality::<Color>(), 3);

# first in enum_iterator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enum-iterator/latest/target-redirect/enum_iterator/fn.first.html

## Expand description

Returns the first value of type `T`.

Same as [ Sequence::first](https://docs.rs/trait.Sequence.html#tymethod.first).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enum_iterator::{first, Sequence};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
assert_eq!(first::<Day>(), Some(Day::Monday));
```

# next in enum_iterator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/enum-iterator/latest/target-redirect/enum_iterator/fn.next.html

## Expand description

Returns the next value of type `T` or `None` if this was the end.

Same as [ Sequence::next](https://docs.rs/trait.Sequence.html#tymethod.next).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use enum_iterator::{next, Sequence};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Sequence)]
enum Day { Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday }
assert_eq!(next(&Day::Friday), Some(Day::Saturday));
```

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [arg](https://docs.rs/macro.arg.html)
- Create an `Arg`
- [command](https://docs.rs/macro.command.html)- `cargo`
- Allows you to build the `Command`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_authors.html)- authors - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the authors for the command from your Cargo.toml at
compile time in the form:
`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_description.html)- description - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the description from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_name.html)- name - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_version.html)- version - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the version from your Cargo.toml at compile time as
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`
- [value_](https://docs.rs/macro.value_parser.html)- parser
- Select a `ValueParser`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arg](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.
- [ArgGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgGroup.html)
- Specifies a logical group of [arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- [ArgMatches](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgMatches.html)
- Container for parse results.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- Build a command-line interface.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- `Arg`- `ArgGroup`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ArgAction](https://docs.rs/enum.ArgAction.html)
- Behavior of arguments when they are encountered while parsing
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- Represents the color preferences for program output
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValueHint.html)- Hint
- Provide shell with hint on how to complete an argument.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Args](https://docs.rs/trait.Args.html)
- Parse a set of arguments into a user-defined container.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/trait.CommandFactory.html)- Factory
- Create a `Command`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromArgMatches.html)- ArgMatches
- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.
- [Subcommand](https://docs.rs/trait.Subcommand.html)
- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueEnum.html)- Enum
- Parse arguments into enums.

Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2

## Expand description

`clap` is a simple-to-use, efficient, and full-featured library for parsing command line
arguments and subcommands when writing console/terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user
at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means
you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of
arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) ‘for free’ meaning
automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking the list of valid possibilities you
supplied and adding only the ones you haven’t already defined. If you are using subcommands,
`clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any
applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and
exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to
exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of
the arguments.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`.
For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and
occurrences see the [documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/), [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of
this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl2Z5T8g1pRkIynR3E0_pc7U).

**NOTE:** All of these examples are functionally the same, but show different styles in which to
use `clap`

The first example shows a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it’s more verbose.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is
// more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility
// to generate arguments dynamically.
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("My Super Program")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("config")
                               .short("c")
                               .long("config")
                               .value_name("FILE")
                               .help("Sets a custom config file")
                               .takes_value(true))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT")
                               .help("Sets the input file to use")
                               .required(true)
                               .index(1))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("v")
                               .short("v")
                               .multiple(true)
                               .help("Sets the level of verbosity"))
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg(Arg::with_name("debug")
                                          .short("d")
                                          .help("print debug information verbosely")))
                          .get_matches();
    // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf"
    let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf");
    println!("Value for config: {}", config);
    // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't
    // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value)
    println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap());
    // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag
    // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v'
    match matches.occurrences_of("v") {
        0 => println!("No verbose info"),
        1 => println!("Some verbose info"),
        2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"),
        3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"),
    }
    // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name
    // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time
    if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") {
        if matches.is_present("debug") {
            println!("Printing debug info...");
        } else {
            println!("Printing normally...");
        }
    }
    // more program logic goes here...
}
```
The next example shows a far less verbose method, but sacrifices some of the advanced
configuration options (not shown in this small example). This method also takes a *very* minor
runtime penalty.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments
// which is less verbose
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("myapp")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .args_from_usage(
                              "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file'
                              <INPUT>              'Sets the input file to use'
                              -v...                'Sets the level of verbosity'")
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'"))
                          .get_matches();
    // Same as previous example...
}
```
This third method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization.

First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we
like:

```
name: myapp
version: "1.0"
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: "1.3"
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Since this feature requires additional dependencies that not everyone may want, it is *not*
compiled in by default and we need to enable a feature flag in Cargo.toml:

Simply change your `clap = "~2.27.0"` to `clap = {version = "~2.27.0", features = ["yaml"]}`.

At last we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far
// more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods.
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
    // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found
    let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml");
    let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches();
    // Same as previous examples...
}
```
Finally there is a macro version, which is like a hybrid approach offering the speed of the builder pattern (the first example), but without all the verbosity.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
fn main() {
    let matches = clap_app!(myapp =>
        (version: "1.0")
        (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
        (about: "Does awesome things")
        (@arg CONFIG: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file")
        (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use")
        (@arg debug: -d ... "Sets the level of debugging information")
        (@subcommand test =>
            (about: "controls testing features")
            (version: "1.3")
            (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
            (@arg verbose: -v --verbose "Print test information verbosely")
        )
    ).get_matches();
    // Same as before...
}
```
If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or
`help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

```
$ myprog --help
My Super Program 1.0
Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
Does awesome things
USAGE:
    MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND]
FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints this message
    -v               Sets the level of verbosity
    -V, --version    Prints version information
OPTIONS:
    -c, --config <FILE>    Sets a custom config file
ARGS:
    INPUT    The input file to use
SUBCOMMANDS:
    help    Prints this message
    test    Controls testing features
```
**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the
`test` subcommand.

[dependencies.clap]

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
# Cherry-pick the features you'd like to use
features = [ "suggestions", "color" ]
```

There are a few goals of `clap` that I’d like to maintain throughout contributions. If your
proposed changes break, or go against any of these goals we’ll discuss the changes further
before merging (but will *not* be ignored, all contributes are welcome!). These are by no means
hard-and-fast rules, as I’m no expert and break them myself from time to time (even if by
mistake or ignorance).

- Remain backwards compatible when possible
- If backwards compatibility *must*be broken, use deprecation warnings if at all possible before removing legacy code - This does not apply for security concerns

- If backwards compatibility
- Parse arguments quickly
- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although *slightly*less stringent, as the program is about to exit)

- Parsing of arguments shouldn’t slow down usage of the main program - This is also true of
generating help and usage information (although
- Try to be cognizant of memory usage
- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of `clap`should be low since the main program is the star of the show

- Once parsing is complete, the memory footprint of
- `panic!`on- *developer*error, exit gracefully on- *end-user*error

Because `clap` takes `SemVer` and compatibility seriously, this is the official policy regarding
breaking changes and previous versions of Rust.

`clap` will pin the minimum required version of Rust to the CI builds. Bumping the minimum
version of Rust is considered a minor breaking change, meaning *at a minimum* the minor version
of `clap` will be bumped.

In order to keep from being surprised by breaking changes, it is **highly** recommended to use
the `~major.minor.patch` style in your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies] clap = "~2.27.0"
```
This will cause *only* the patch version to be updated upon a `cargo update` call, and therefore
cannot break due to new features, or bumped minimum versions of Rust.

`clap` will officially support current stable Rust, minus two releases, but may work with prior
releases as well. For example, current stable Rust at the time of this writing is 1.21.0,
meaning `clap` is guaranteed to compile with 1.19.0 and beyond. At the 1.22.0 release, `clap`
will be guaranteed to compile with 1.20.0 and beyond, etc.

Upon bumping the minimum version of Rust (assuming it’s within the stable-2 range), it *must* be
clearly annotated in the `CHANGELOG.md`

`clap` is licensed under the MIT license. Please read the [LICENSE-MIT](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v2.34.0/LICENSE-MIT) file in
this repository for more information.
